The difference in the results between SVAR and SDFM is attributed to the limitation of small-scale SVARs. Since small-scale SVARs potentially suffer from limited information problem due to inclusion of few variables in the model, the VAR innovations may not span the space of the structural shocks, and therefore may not recover the true IRFs. This leads to the estimation of distorted IRFs. As noted in the literature, Bernanke and Kuttner (2005) and Nakamura and 20 Figure 3: IRF of Government Spending Shocks on Selected Variables using SVAR Model Steinsson, 2018) show that incorporating a large information set in a dynamic factor model leads to estimating significant effects as compared to a benchmark VAR. The main contribution of this paper is combining two important econometric methods (coin-tegration and dynamic factor models) to estimate the response of asset prices (stock price and house price) to government spending shocks.

results.title: Global identification, estimation and inference of structural impulse response functions in factor models: A unified framework - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Global identification, estimation and inference of structural impulse response functions in factor models: A unified framework☆. This paper develops a theory for the global identification, estimation and inference of impulse response functions (IRFs) in structural factor models (SFMs). A new theorem is established to address IRF identification under both recursive and nonrecursive schemes in SFMs. Moreover, we develop two new estimators for structural IRFs under principal component normalization and establish their asymptotic distributions. This paper addresses several interrelated issues regarding the identification, estimation, and inference of structural IRFs. First, although the structural VAR (SVAR) literature provides extensive results regarding the identification of structural IRFs, modifications are necessary when applying them to SFMs. In contrast to SVARs, SFMs have unique features that require a normalization scheme for unobserved factors and loadings before imposing identifying restrictions. (2010) establish conditions only for recursively identified shocks, leaving a gap in our understanding of nonrecursive partial identification within SFMs. Third, as existing estimators of structural IRFs are primarily designed for specific identification schemes, the literature lacks a general estimator and corresponding asymptotic theory for IRFs in SFMs under general (possibly overidentifying) conditions. To address these issues, we develop a theory for the global identification of structural IRFs in SFMs and propose estimators under both full and partial identification schemes, including those with potentially overidentifying restrictions. For identification in factor models, Bai and Ng (2013) propose three just-identified schemes for identifying factors and loadings in factor models, but they do not address the identification of structural IRFs in SFMs. Bai et al. Section 3 examines the effects of normalization, develops a theory of global identification of structural IRFs in SFMs, and establishes a theory of partial identification under nonrecursive restrictions. This section develops two estimators for structural IRFs under identification schemes that satisfy Properties (1) and (2), allowing for the commonly used PC1 normalization. results.title: Factor Analysis Model - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: A factor analysis model is defined as a statistical framework used to identify latent variables (common factors) that explain the covariances or correlations among manifest variables, partitioning the variance of each manifest variable into common and unique components. The covariance matrix for these observed categorical variables will not fit the common factor model, or factor analysis of observations on these variables will yield biased factor loadings. Factor analysis (FA) refers to a set of latent variable models and methods for fitting them to data. The model could be fitted to a matrix of correlations instead of covariances; this standardizes the factor loadings and elements of **D**ψ. The covariance matrix for these observed categorical variables will not fit the common factor model, or factor analysis of observations on these variables will yield biased factor loadings. With the factor analysis model, we avoid having to compute the inverses of iterates of the estimated *p* × *p* covariance matrix that may be singular for large *p* relative to *n*.
